entries.topic: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo: the vines the rule names
entries.claim: Question c-ndvwbnke says the denomination permits Bombino Bianco as well as Trebbiano Abruzzese; the Italy country record says Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a different grape from Trebbiano Toscano, while the Abruzzo record says the wine may be made from Trebbiano Abruzzese and Trebbiano Toscano, at least 85 per cent together.
entries.finding: The rule of 1972 named Trebbiano d'Abruzzo with Bombino Bianco, the two long confused in the vineyard. The disciplinare approved by ministerial decree of 19 January 2023 (Gazzetta Ufficiale of 6 February 2023) names Trebbiano Abruzzese and/or Trebbiano Toscano, at least 85 per cent, and no longer Bombino Bianco; the region's comparison of texts of December 2024 says Article 2 no longer provides for Bombino, and reports of the ordinary amendment approved in August 2026 give the same base. Trebbiano Abruzzese the vine is distinct from Trebbiano Toscano; the wine Trebbiano d'Abruzzo may be made from either.

refuter.note: The base of the rule holds: the region's own bulletin of December 2024 sets out the text in force, the disciplinare as amended by the decree of 19 January 2023 (G.U. no. 30 of 6 February 2023), and it reads Trebbiano Abruzzese and/or Trebbiano Toscano at least 85 per cent, the sub-zones 90; Federdoc's listing of 2020 still read Trebbiano Abruzzese and/or Bombino Bianco and/or Trebbiano Toscano. So Bombino left the named base between 2020 and the 2023 text, but nothing read shows the 2023 decree itself made that cut, and the search summaries did not show the bulletin's own words on Bombino that the finding quotes. The new explanation of c-ndvwbnke therefore says the rule as amended in January 2023 names the two Trebbianos (true whichever decree dropped Bombino) in place of since January 2023. Its stem, answer and accept list stay true: the stem speaks of what reaches the bottle, the explanation keeps the vineyard confusion that puts Bombino Bianco there, and the accept list takes Trebbiano Abruzzese. country.grapes[10].styles: may use either read loosely and now reads may be made from either. entries.claim: The Lombardy, Marche and Italy records, two questions, a producer note and the Trebbiano and Verdicchio grape pages say Lugana's Turbiana (once Trebbiano di Lugana) is Verdicchio, the same vine as Trebbiano di Soave.
entries.finding: For Trebbiano di Soave every source agrees it is Verdicchio. For Turbiana the studies differ: the Vitis study of 2001 found Trebbiano di Soave identical to Verdicchio and Trebbiano di Lugana very similar; a study in Advances in Horticultural Science (2012) found one DNA profile across 25 accessions, a Turbiana among them; the Lugana consortium treats Turbiana as a distinct vine closely related to Verdicchio, which is why Lugana took the name. So Turbiana is so close to Verdicchio that it is often taught as the same vine, but not proven identical.

entries.why: Only the Turbiana half was overstated: Trebbiano di Soave stays Verdicchio everywhere (the Veneto record and friuli's r-ls1a2rd8 are right), the accept list of r-uf2jj6ug keeps Verdicchio, the Marche styles line already says DNA ties it and stays, and the Verdicchio page's aliases and regions list keep Turbiana by the grape plan.

refuter.note: Tried to refute the softening from both sides. Towards identity: the national register files Turbiana and Trebbiano di Lugana as synonyms of Trebbiano di Soave, itself filed under Verdicchio Bianco, and the 2012 study found one profile across 25 accessions, a Turbiana among them. Towards a separate vine: the consortium has held since its announcement of 2021 that Turbiana is a distinct vine closely related to Verdicchio, has registered Turbiana clones of its own, and two trade reports call it a biotype. Identity is unproven either way, so so close to Verdicchio in DNA studies that it is often taught as the same vine, and tied by DNA, are true on every reading; Trebbiano di Soave stays Verdicchio. Paths: three targets in trebbiano.json named the wrong index; the strings sit at labels[4].means, compare[1].tell and cards[1].back, now corrected. profile.confuse: Lugana's its near twin read as a fragment and now reads Trebbiano di Soave is Verdicchio, Lugana's Turbiana nearly so, which keeps the line at the page's cap of 30 words. Every old string occurs once in its file. Answers stay true: r-uf2jj6ug answers Turbiana and may keep Verdicchio in its accept list while the register files the names as one vine; c-7zyl7br8 answers Turbiana; c-lhywvj93 answers Trebbiano di Soave. Left for the owner: the Verdicchio page's questions[1] stem asks for a wine of the same grape as a Lugana; not shown wrong while the register treats them as one, so it stays. Completeness: a grep of js/, the region fragments, the CMS, the rewrite banks and the grape pages finds no further place that states Turbiana is Verdicchio; the Marche styles line, the Verdicchio page's label row, guest answer and profile, and friuli's r-ls1a2rd8 already say tied, as near as makes no difference, or Lugana's grape; the Trebbiano page's notIn line sits in its report, which never ships.

entries.topic: Sicily: the 2017 rule and Grillo's billing
entries.claim: The Sicily record says in six places that varietal Nero d'Avola and Grillo must be Sicilia DOC since 2017, while its card cards[6] and question r-ih3gzpr1 say the names belong to the island's DOCs, Sicilia above all; three lines call Grillo the island's best dry or varietal white.
entries.finding: The change in force from the 2017 harvest amended the Terre Siciliane IGT rule: Grillo and Calabrese (Nero d'Avola) may no longer be named on an IGT label, in varietal or optional information. It reserves nothing to Sicilia DOC alone: the island's other DOCs still name the grapes, Noto DOC for one keeps a Noto Nero d'Avola of at least 85 per cent, and Eloro and Vittoria name it too. A challenge before the regional administrative court was overturned by the Council of State, which upheld the change. Calling Grillo the island's best white is a judgement the house rules keep out.

refuter.note: The rule holds as the entry gives it: the amended Terre Siciliane text bars IGT Grillo and Nero d'Avola from the 2017 vintage, the Council of State upheld it, and the consortium's director said the two belong to every Sicilian DOC that names them, not to Sicilia alone; the trade reports of 2017 agree. Two new texts named Noto and Vittoria as DOCs for both grapes, but those name Nero d'Avola and no Grillo type was found in either; Erice DOC has a Grillo type of its own. traps[7] and the CMS explanation now name Erice for Grillo and Noto for Nero d'Avola. Nothing else moves: the other six read well in place, cards[6] and r-ih3gzpr1 already agree, e-l2zcmjow still answers Sicilia DOC on a stem that says unless a smaller DOC applies, and every old string occurs once. Grillo as a cross of Catarratto and Zibibbo stands. Completeness: the Nero d'Avola page already says a DOC, most often Sicilia DOC; no other file says Sicilia DOC alone since 2017, and no other place calls Grillo the island's best. Also tested and left: Nero d'Avola as the island's most planted red (still so on the 2021 register figures, see L2-09), and Etna's DOCG, which the record gives as applied for and pending; a report of September 2026 still calls it the next milestone. entries.finding: No measurement across Italy's varieties was found that ranks Sagrantino first. One study of Sagrantino wines found the highest mean oligomeric procyanidins among the wines it compared, 1.2 g/L against 0.8 g/L for Nebbiolo, a result inside one study's sample. Trade and grape references agree on the substance: small, thick skinned berries and a tannin and polyphenol load that puts it among the most tannic of all grapes.

Left: ADV a-dq2mo3wg, whose stem asks for Sagrantino's claim to fame, a reputation, so its answer stands; i-70avillq (one of Italy's most tannic) and the CMS's two of Italy's most tannic reds are already hedged.

refuter.note: The finding says no measurement ranks Sagrantino first across Italy's varieties; one does, within its sample. A survey of 110 single variety wines of eleven Italian red grapes from one vintage (Food Research International, 2021) found Sagrantino highest in total phenolics, 3578 mg/L, and richest in proanthocyanidins and vanillin reactive flavanols, with Corvina lowest at 1065. So the record's measured claim was nearer the truth than the finding allows, but in any Italian variety and the most tannic grape in Italy still reach past eleven grapes and one vintage, and the change stands. The new texts said among the most tannic of all grapes, the very shape of the house rule's own example of a forbidden superlative (most tannic in the world); they now use the comparative the reviewed Sagrantino grape page already uses (more tannin than almost any grape), which both sources bear out. cards[5].b still answers its front (why Sagrantino is famous among grapes). Every old string occurs once; the producer style line sits in a single quoted string, so its new text carries no apostrophe. Should the owner want the measured rank kept, it would need the survey added to the Umbria record's sources: the highest tannin and polyphenol load of eleven Italian reds measured side by side in 2021. Left, and agreed: ADV a-dq2mo3wg, whose stem asks the grape's claim to fame; i-70avillq (one of Italy's most tannic red grapes) and the CMS's two of Italy's most tannic reds, both hedged and both now borne out by the survey. Completeness: Aglianico's and Tannat's GRAPES_PLUS rows compare grip without a rank; no other place ranks Sagrantino.

sources.title: Food Research International 143 (2021) 110277: a survey of the diversity of Italian red wines by their oenological parameters, colour and phenolic indices
sources.says: 110 monovarietal wines of eleven Italian red varieties, one vintage: Sagrantino highest in total phenolics (3578 mg/L) and richest in proanthocyanidins and vanillin reactive flavanols; Corvina lowest (1065 mg/L).

entries.claim: INTRO_GRAPES gives Garganega acid 2 of 3, medium, beside a trap line of gentle almond and stone fruit.
entries.finding: References place Garganega's acidity from medium to high, centred on medium plus: the Soave consortium describes a late ripener harvested well into October whose blend partner, Trebbiano di Soave, brings freshness with its malic acid; a sommelier body's study of the Veneto gives the best dry Soave moderate plus acidity; some grape profiles say high. On this dial 3 is the mark of the grapes taught as high acid (Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Albariño, Assyrtiko, Furmint, Melon, Cortese, Verdejo, Grüner Veltliner) and 2 covers medium to medium plus (Chardonnay, Vermentino, Pinot Blanc, Silvaner, Glera).

sources.title: Consorzio Tutela Vini Soave: the grapes
sources.says: Garganega ripens late and is harvested well into October; Trebbiano di Soave ripens earlier and its high malic acid adds freshness to the blend.

sources.title: GuildSomm: Italy's Adriatic Coast, Part 1, Veneto and the DOCG
sources.says: The best dry Soave and Gambellara are crisp, with moderate plus acidity, yet textural.

sources.title: Primal Wine: Garganega, grape varietal profile
sources.says: Acidity medium to high.

entries.why: Medium plus sits in 2 on this three step dial, which keeps 3 for the sharp whites and keeps Soave the softer foil to Gavi (Cortese 3) and Verdicchio, as the Garganega and Verdicchio grape pages teach it (medium to medium plus); 2 stands.

refuter.note: Read the dial against itself: INTRO_GRAPES gives acid 3 to Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Grüner Veltliner, Albariño, Verdejo, Cortese, Furmint, Assyrtiko and Melon de Bourgogne, and 2 to Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Sémillon, Torrontés, Roussanne, Vermentino, Glera, Silvaner and Pinot Blanc. Decanter's guide to ageing Italian whites puts Garganega with Fiano and Vermentino among the whites less aggressive in acidity, with Verdicchio between the groups; a wine school's guide gives the grape good acidity. With Vermentino at 2, Garganega at 2 is the consistent mark, and the Garganega page's medium to medium plus and its compare line (Verdicchio sharper) agree. The trap line's gentle almond and stone fruit speaks of flavour, not acidity. Leave stands.

sources.title: Decanter: ageing Italian whites, a patient wine lover's guide (May 2020)
sources.says: Groups Fiano, Garganega and Vermentino as more phenolic, less aggressive in acidity and richer in body; Verdicchio shares traits with both groups.

entries.topic: Lambrusco at the table: cold, and the flute
entries.claim: The Emilia-Romagna record says serve Lambrusco cold in a flute or a white wine glass (exam[6], cards[7].b), the Sorbara cold (wines[0].note) and the amabile well chilled (wines[3].note); the grape table gives 10 to 14 degrees Celsius after Gambero Rosso.
entries.finding: The Court's own Certified syllabus cell, transcribed in .scripts/cms/subjects/lombardy-emilia-romagna.json, says Lambrusco is served as any other sparkling wine, cold and in a flute or wine glass, and the CMS question e-ltbv1b5r teaches it so. The Consorzio Tutela Lambrusco serves Lambrusco DOC at 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; Gambero Rosso's guidelines for restaurateurs give 10 for Sorbara and the rosés and 14 for the dark wines; a producer's sheet gives 6 to 8 for an amabile rosato. So cold holds for the run of Lambrusco and the pale Sorbara, the flute stands on the Court's word, and well chilled holds for the sweet amabile; only the dark Grasparossa runs warmer, which the grape table already says.

sources.title: Court of Master Sommeliers Americas: Introductory Sommelier Course and Certified Sommelier Theory Exam Curriculum Guide (CMS-A 8.2023), pages 28 and 29, Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna, Service of Beverage
sources.says: Certified cell: Lambrusco is served as you would any other sparkling wine, cold and in a flute or wine glass, with the Court's published sparkling wine service standards (read in the Codex's transcription, .scripts/cms/subjects/lombardy-emilia-romagna.json).

sources.title: Consorzio Tutela Lambrusco: Lambrusco DOC a spicchi, the pizza tour
sources.says: Serve the Emilian bubbles at the right temperature, between 8 and 10 degrees Celsius.

sources.title: Gambero Rosso: Lambrusco at the restaurant, a decalogue for restaurateurs
sources.says: 14 degrees for the dark Lambruscos, 10 for Sorbara and the rosés.

sources.title: Ceci 1938: technical sheet of a Lambrusco Emilia IGT rosato amabile
sources.says: Serving temperature 6 to 8 degrees for the amabile rosato.

entries.why: The sources do not agree on cool: the Court and the consortium put Lambrusco cold, 8 to 10 degrees, and the Court names the flute; the record follows the Court word for word and stays. For the owner: the grape table's 10 to 14 is Gambero Rosso's figure and misses the consortium's 8; widening it to 8 to 14 would need the consortium among that page's sources, which already stand at their cap of four.

refuter.note: Searched for a consortium text that puts Lambrusco cool or bans the flute and found none: trade pages split (a Lambrusco writer prefers a tumbler or a Bordeaux stem to a flute, one product sheet gives 6 to 8 degrees for a rosé, one article 15 to 18 for a dark red), which is a spread of habit, not a fault in the record. The record follows the Court's Certified cell word for word (cold, a flute or a wine glass), the Sorbara and amabile notes sit at the cold end every source gives for those styles, and the Grasparossa note names no temperature. The grape page's 10 to 14, pale Sorbara cooler and dark Grasparossa warmer, does not contradict cold for the run of Lambrusco. Leave stands.

entries.topic: Planting ranks: Montepulciano in Abruzzo and Italy, Nero d'Avola in Sicily
entries.claim: The Abruzzo record calls Montepulciano one of the most planted reds of Italy and almost the whole of Abruzzo's red vineyard (grapes[0].styles); the Sicily record calls Nero d'Avola the island's most planted red (grapes[0].styles).
entries.finding: A survey of the Abruzzo vineyard reported by the regional consortium puts Montepulciano at over 52 per cent of all 33,964 hectares, with Trebbiano Toscano second at about 14 per cent and the rest spread over 118 varieties, most of them white; no figure for the red share alone was found, but almost the whole reads true. Italian planting tables of 2015 and later put Montepulciano second of the reds, behind Sangiovese, at about 27,000 hectares. The Sicilian register figures of 2021 give Nero d'Avola 15,387 hectares, second on the island to Catarratto and first of the reds.

sources.title: Consorzio Tutela Vini d'Abruzzo: brochure of the vineyard survey (2025)
sources.says: Montepulciano over 52 per cent of the Abruzzo vineyard.

sources.title: Gambero Rosso: a vineyard map defines the Abruzzo territory's suitability
sources.says: Over 155,000 parcels, 33,964 hectares and 118 varieties; Montepulciano over 52 per cent of the whole vineyard, Trebbiano Toscano second at about 14.

sources.title: BKWine: the most popular grape varieties in Italy
sources.says: Sangiovese about 54,000 hectares; Montepulciano and Glera about 27,000 each, then Pinot Grigio and Merlot (24,000): Montepulciano the second red.

sources.title: QdS: Nero d'Avola, the king of Sicilian wines (SIAN figures of 2021)
sources.says: Of 97,080 hectares of Sicilian vineyard in 2021, Nero d'Avola holds 15,387; another count puts it second to Catarratto.

entries.why: Both ranks were flagged as volatile (check-g10, check-g11) and both still hold on the figures read; one of the most planted is already hedged, and almost the whole fits a grape holding over half of all the region's vines. Left, as L1-12 and L3-07 left the ranks that hold.

refuter.note: Added by the second reader so that every Italy flag in the codexRecords notes has an entry: check-g10 flagged the Abruzzo share and check-g11 the Sicily rank. Tested both against current figures and found them true; nothing is written. The Abruzzo record's other strong words (the most reliable value in a wines note, the two most celebrated and most famous estates) and Umbria's the most famous of them were not flagged and are left for the owner.
